sections.heading: Initial Problem in the InfyTel Application

items: The application allows a customer to enroll in Prepaid or Postpaid plans.
The Customer class directly instantiates Prepaid or Postpaid, causing tight coupling.
The above code:
Create a common interface Plan, implemented by both Prepaid and Postpaid.
Benefits:
Instead of the Customer creating the Plan, the Plan is passed from the outside.
Object control is inverted – from Customer → Prepaid to Prepaid → Customer.
Eliminates tight coupling.
Easier to unit test using mock dependencies.
Improves maintainability and flexibility.

sections.heading: Scaling Problem with IoC and Manual Injection

items: Manually managing multiple dependencies becomes complex and error-prone.
Need for automation leads to Dependency Injection frameworks.
Definition: DI frameworks take responsibility for:
Popular DI Frameworks:
Spring is the most widely used DI framework in Java applications.

rows: Dependencies are passed via the class constructor.
Dependencies are set using public setter methods.
Dependencies are injected directly into fields (discouraged in Spring).

items: In Spring:
Tight coupling in code leads to rigidity and poor testability.
Inversion of Control (IoC) inverts object creation to achieve better design.
Dependency Injection (DI) is a practical implementation of IoC.
Using frameworks like Spring, we automate dependency management, simplify testing, and increase modularity.
